result: {"decisions":[{"point":"D1","problem":"How to decide which attacks a defense evaluation must include to show real robustness rather than robustness to known attacks only.","did":"Required that evaluators actively attempt to evade the specific defense with adaptive attacks after fully specifying it, rather than only testing against prior fixed attacks.","alternatives_named":["evaluating only against previous or state-of-the-art attacks not targeting the specific defense"],"stated_reason":"A defense only matters if it withstands future attacks; defeating a fixed attack is easy to achieve by subtly breaking that attack (like rot-14 vs rot-13), and non-adaptive attacks are already solved.","quote":"The first, and by far most important, component of a defense evaluation is to attempt to evade the specific defense. After the defense has been defined, ask: what attack could possibly defeat this defense?"},{"point":"D2","problem":"Which attack strength and type to use when evaluating a defense's robustness, given that weak attacks can be defeated by gradient masking.","did":"Recommended against relying on Fast Gradient Sign alone, and instead advised iterative attacks with 1000+ iterations.","alternatives_named":["Fast Gradient Sign exclusively","10 or 100 iterations of gradient descent"],"stated_reason":"FGS was never intended as a strong attack and weak adversarial training can defeat it via gradient masking; no reasonable threat model lets an attacker run 100 iterations but not 1000.","quote":"There is no reasonable threat model under which an attacker can compute 10 (or 100) iterations of gradient descent, but not 1000. Because the threat model must not constrain the approach an attacker takes, it is always worth evaluating against a strong attack with many iterations of gradient descent."},{"point":"D2","problem":"How to detect whether a defense is causing gradient masking that fools gradient-based attacks.","did":"Recommended also running gradient-free attacks (ZOO, SPSA, NES, decision-only) to check for gradient masking.","alternatives_named":["ZOO","SPSA","NES","Decision-only adversarial example generation"],"stated_reason":"To ensure the model is not causing various forms of gradient masking.","quote":"Apply gradient-free attacks. To ensure that the model is not causing various forms of gradient masking, it is worth attempting gradient-free attacks. There are several such proposals. I would recommend these four."},{"point":"D2","problem":"How to confirm that the attack suite is not missing obvious adversarial examples.","did":"Recommended brute-force random search attacks as a sanity check, with a few hundred thousand random samples on about a hundred instances.","alternatives_named":["gradient-based attacks","gradient-free attacks"],"stated_reason":"Random sampling confirms nothing obvious is missed, and if it finds adversarial examples other methods missed, then the other attacks can be improved.","quote":"If brute-force random sampling identifies adversarial examples that other methods haven't found, this indicates that other attacks can be improved."},{"point":"D3","problem":"Whether to accept an iterative attack's results when they look worse than a simpler single-step attack.","did":"Advised treating an iterative attack that underperforms a single-step attack as likely incorrect, and diagnosing it with plots of success rate and loss vs. iterations.","alternatives_named":["accepting the weaker iterative attack results at face value"],"stated_reason":"Iterative attacks are strictly more powerful than single-step attacks, so underperformance suggests the attack is flawed or the model is obfuscating gradients.","quote":"Iterative attacks are strictly more powerful than single-step attacks, and so their results should be strictly superior. If an iterative attack performs worse than a single-step attack, this often indicates that the iterative attack is not correct."},{"point":"D3","problem":"Whether to accept an attack evaluation as sound when white-box attacks do worse than black-box attacks.","did":"Advised treating black-box attacks outperforming white-box attacks as a sign of gradient masking or a weak white-box attack, and investigating the instances where only black-box succeeds.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"White-box attacks are a strict superset of black-box attacks, so they should perform strictly better.","quote":"Because white-box attacks are a strict superset of black-box attacks, they should perform strictly better. Black-box attacks doing better often indicates that the defense is somehow masking gradient information."},{"point":"D3","problem":"How to decide whether an attack is correctly implemented using sanity checks on unbounded and increasing-distortion settings.","did":"Advised verifying that attack success increases monotonically with distortion and that unbounded attacks reach 100% success, treating violations as evidence of a flawed attack.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"More distortion makes attacks strictly stronger, and with unbounded distortion any attack should eventually succeed, so violations indicate incorrect application.","quote":"Verify that unbounded attacks always succeed. With unbounded distortion, any attack should eventually reach 100% success, if only by switching the input to actually be part of the other class."},{"point":"D5","problem":"How to compare defenses when one performs better on weak attacks but worse on strong ones, and how to compare across different attack regimes.","did":"Recommended judging defenses by the worst-case (strongest) attack and not comparing numbers from fixed-attack evaluations against adaptive-attack evaluations.","alternatives_named":["comparing defenses on weaker attacks such as FGS","comparing fixed-attack numbers of a new defense to adaptive-attack numbers of prior defenses"],"stated_reason":"Comparing across different attack strengths is unfair, like comparing MLP accuracy on MNIST to ResNet accuracy on CIFAR.","quote":"If Defense A does better than Defense B on weaker attacks (e.g., FGS) but does worse against a stronger attack (e.g., PGD), then Defense B is the stronger defense."}]}
